name: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Healthcare
answer: The AI enablement audit in healthcare is a structured review of whether a clinical AI tool is fit to be used, and whether the organisation around it is ready to run it safely. It covers the model itself, the data it was trained and validated on, the way it is deployed, and the human and paper processes that catch its mistakes. It sits inside governance, compliance and medical device security work, and it is distinct from a clinical trial, because the question is not only whether the tool works but whether this hospital can operate it. The audit produces a record that regulators, accreditation bodies and internal risk committees can inspect.

sections.body: The AI enablement audit in healthcare is a structured review of whether a clinical AI tool is fit to be used, and whether the organisation around it is ready to run it safely. It covers the model itself, the data it was trained and validated on, the way it is deployed, and the human and paper processes that catch its mistakes. It sits inside governance, compliance and medical device security work, and it is distinct from a clinical trial, because the question is not only whether the tool works but whether this hospital can operate it. The audit produces a record that regulators, accreditation bodies and internal risk committees can inspect.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The audit runs on the same estate the tool will touch: the electronic health record, the imaging archive, the laboratory and scheduling systems, and the interfaces that move data between them. It also depends on identity and access management, audit logging, version control for models and prompts, and the environment where the tool is hosted, whether that is on premises, in a private cloud or through a vendor. Evidence lives in document stores, ticketing systems and configuration repositories, and the audit is only as good as the traceability of those records. Where a tool is regulated as a medical device, the technical file and post market surveillance data feed the same review.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done by a small team, usually drawn from clinical informatics, security, compliance and the clinical service that will use the tool. They start with a description of intended use and the population it will serve, then check training and validation data for representativeness and leakage, and test performance on local data where that is possible. They review the vendor's documentation, the device classification, the cybersecurity posture and the integration design, then walk through failure modes with the clinicians who will see the output. Findings are logged, assigned and closed, and the audit is repeated when the model, the data or the workflow changes. Much of the effort is in interviews and document review rather than in code.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Ownership has to be clear before the audit starts: who signs off, who monitors performance after go live, and who can switch the tool off. The audit maps the tool against medical device rules, data protection law, professional guidance and local policy, and it records consent, data sharing and retention arrangements. It also examines what happens when the tool is wrong, including how a clinician can override it, how the event is reported and how the vendor is notified. Provenance matters throughout, from the source of training data to the version of the model in use and the changes made since it was approved. The output is a defensible record, not a guarantee, and it should be readable by people who are not engineers.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Audit practice is moving from one off approval toward continuous monitoring, with performance drift, bias and safety signals checked on a schedule rather than once. Regulators are asking for clearer post market evidence, and buyers are asking vendors for documentation that maps to recognised frameworks rather than bespoke questionnaires. Automation will help with evidence collection and logging, but the judgement about local fitness will stay with the clinical and governance teams. Expect more attention to foundation models and third party components that a single tool quietly depends on, and to the contracts that determine who can inspect what. The direction is toward audits that are repeatable, comparable and tied to the real workflow they are meant to protect.
